feedback: If a learner calls the finds dinosaurs, have Anning gently correct: 'No, those were sea reptiles — they swam in the ocean and are a separate group from dinosaurs.'
If a learner thinks fossil hunting was a safe hobby, have her describe the dangerous, crumbling cliffs (a cliff-fall killed her dog Tray) and that she sold fossils to feed her family.
If a learner assumes she was a trained, wealthy scientist, have her explain she was self-taught and largely outside the formal scientific world.
If a learner thinks she was always famous, have her explain that much of her work was published by men without naming her and that recognition came largely later.
Affirm answers that connect a named find (ichthyosaur or plesiosaur) to why it mattered: evidence that creatures once lived that no longer exist.
activities.intendedInsight: Mary Anning was a real person whose discoveries were key evidence that whole kinds of animals had gone extinct — a radical idea at the time — and whose lack of credit as a poor woman raises the question of who gets to do science and who gets remembered.
learnerActions: Picture standing on the windy shingle beach at Lyme Regis while Mary Anning works the cliffs, and ask her questions such as 'What did you find?', 'Was it dangerous?', and 'Why wasn't your name on the discoveries?'

Listen to her describe how her brother Joseph found a strange giant ichthyosaur skull (around 1811) and how she, as a girl of about 12, found and dug out the rest of the skeleton, and how she later uncovered the first nearly complete plesiosaur skeleton (1823)
Ask her why fossil hunting was risky and hear about working the crumbling sea cliffs and the landslides that endangered fossil hunters — one cliff-fall killed her dog Tray and nearly killed her

Ask her why her name was often missing from the discoveries and hear, plainly, that gentlemen bought her fossils and wrote scientific papers about them, often without naming her as the finder, and that as a woman she could not even join the Geological Society
Ask 'Were they dinosaurs?' and hear her correction that her famous beasts were sea reptiles, not dinosaurs
Retell, in your own words, one thing she found and one reason she matters
activities.title: Meet Mary Anning in her own voice

feedback: If a learner labels an uncovered specimen a dinosaur, correct: it is a sea reptile, a separate group.
Reinforce that real cliff hunting was dangerous and that Anning sold finds to survive, so it was work, not a safe hobby.
activities.intendedInsight: A felt sense of what Anning actually did in the field — careful searching, uncovering, and identifying specimens — and that this was hazardous, hands-on work.
learnerActions: Prospect a cliff scene safely to search for fossils where Anning worked
Uncover an ichthyosaur or plesiosaur specimen
Log and label the find as Anning did, noting that it is a marine reptile
Discuss what makes this hunting dangerous (crumbling cliffs, landslides)
activities.title: Prospect the Jurassic Coast like Anning

feedback: Full understanding: names a discovery, explains her finds gave evidence for extinction and prehistoric life, AND distinguishes marine reptiles from dinosaurs.
Partial: names a discovery and says she was important but cannot say why, or still calls her finds dinosaurs — prompt for the 'why it mattered' and the reptile/dinosaur distinction.
Gap: recalls only 'found fossils' or 'found dinosaurs' — reteach using the story and the cliff/timeline.
If a learner says 'she just picked up pretty rocks; it wasn't real science,' connect her specimens to the scientific debates of the time: experts used them to understand extinction and ancient life.
If a learner assumes extinction was already accepted, set the context: the idea that whole kinds of creatures had vanished was new and contested, and her fossils helped establish it.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall of place, era, a named find, and the significance (evidence for extinction and prehistoric life), while distinguishing marine reptiles from dinosaurs.
learnerActions: Match each find to its name (ichthyosaur, plesiosaur)
Answer why her work mattered and why she was often overlooked

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'Mary Anning dug up the skeleton of an ichthyosaur — a giant sea creature no one had ever seen alive. Why was a discovery like this so important for science? And does finding it make Mary Anning a dinosaur hunter?'
Explain in your own words whether ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs were dinosaurs
activities.title: Check the key facts and the big 'why'
